summary: Defines a profile for proxy certificates, which are X.509 certificates signed by an ordinary end-user certificate rather than by a certificate authority. They let a user delegate limited rights to a program or process without sharing their private key. This is useful for single sign-on across systems.

eli5.summary: You sign a note saying your helper may do a few chores for you today. The note expires soon, so you never hand over your real keys.

questions: how do x509 proxy certificates work
subtitle: How a user can sign a short-lived, restricted certificate for a helper program, with no CA involved and no private key shared.

tldr.problem: A user often needs programs and remote services to act on their behalf, but handing over the long-term private key of their X.509 certificate is dangerous, and asking a certificate authority for every new identity is slow.
tldr.mechanism: A Proxy Certificate is signed by the user's own end entity certificate (or by another proxy certificate). It has its own key pair, a name made by appending one Common Name to the issuer's name, and a critical ProxyCertInfo extension that can limit how far and for what it may be used.
tldr.outcome: The user enters a password or smartcard once, delegation needs no third party, and a stolen proxy does not expose the user's real key. This RFC is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no replacement.

facts.value: MUST be present and critical in a PC

today: RFC 3820 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It remains the profile for X.509 proxy certificates, built on RFC 3280.

sections.title: What a Proxy Certificate Is
sections.content:
A proxy in security means that entity A lets entity B be authorized with others as if it were A. RFC 3820 defines a certificate profile for this, built on the X.509 certificates of RFC 3280 (RFC 3280).

A Proxy Certificate (PC) is an X.509 certificate signed by a normal end entity certificate (EEC) or by another PC. The signer is called the Proxy Issuer (PI). Besides plain, unrestricted proxying, the profile defines a framework for carrying policies that limit proxying, and PCs with unique names derived from the EEC name.
sections.eli5: It is a permission slip. You write it yourself, sign it with your own signature, and give it to someone who needs to act for you.

sections.title: Why Delegate With Certificates
sections.content:
The RFC's running example is Steve, an engineer who wants a file transfer service to move large files between hosts while he is offline. The service must authenticate to storage hosts as Steve, and those hosts must authenticate to each other. That needs two things: single sign-on (use the smartcard password once, not for every step) and delegation (remote processes act for Steve).

Proxying lets the smartcard key be used just once, to create the proxy credential. The RFC also gives the background: Grid computing, where the Globus Grid Security Infrastructure introduced in 1997 used proxy certificates similar to these, and this document migrates that experience into a standard.

Two further motivations are stated. A compromised delegate should be limited, so a proxy can carry restrictions such as read-only access to specific files, plus a short lifetime. And a proxy needs its own unique identity so it can be named in policy, which the RFC gets by deriving the name from an existing identity, which needs no third party.
sections.eli5: Imagine giving a babysitter a note that only lets them open the fridge, not the whole house, and only for tonight. If they lose it, you do not have to change your own locks.

sections.title: Properties and Creation of a PC
sections.content:
The RFC lists six properties of a PC. It is signed by an EEC or another PC. It can sign only another PC, never an EEC. It has its own key pair. Its identity is derived from the signing EEC's identity, and it may inherit that EEC's rights subject to the restrictions placed on it. It is nonetheless unique, so it can hold rights independently. And it carries a new extension that identifies it as a PC and holds its policy.

Creation takes three steps: generate a new key pair, build a request for a PC from that key pair, and have the EEC or another PC sign the response after checking the request. When delegating from A to B, B does the first two steps and sends the request to A over an authenticated, integrity-checked channel. A signs and returns the PC. This means private keys never travel: B never sees A's key, and A never sees B's new key.

The RFC contrasts this with Kerberos tickets: a ticket-granting ticket needs a Key Distribution Center, while a PC can be created unilaterally with no third party.
sections.eli5: Your helper draws their own secret stamp and shows you only the print. You approve the print and sign it. Nobody ever sees anyone else's stamp.

sections.title: Certificate Fields and the ProxyCertInfo Extension
sections.content:
Every PC MUST include the critical ProxyCertInfo extension, and a certificate that is not a PC MUST NOT have it. Field rules from section 3:

  • The issuer field MUST contain the subject of the Proxy Issuer, which MUST NOT have an empty subject.
  • The subject is the issuer's subject with a single Common Name appended, which SHOULD be unique among PCs from that issuer.
  • issuerAltName and subjectAltName MUST NOT be present.
  • The cA field in basic constraints MUST NOT be TRUE.
  • The serial number SHOULD be unique among PCs from that issuer.
  • If the issuer has a KeyUsage extension, the Digital Signature bit MUST be asserted.

The extension has an optional pCPathLenConstraint, the maximum depth of PCs that may be signed below this one (0 means this PC must not sign another PC; absent means unlimited), and a required proxyPolicy made of a policyLanguage OID and an optional policy octet string.

Two policy languages MUST be understood by everyone who accepts PCs: id-ppl-inheritAll (unrestricted, inherits all rights and effectively impersonates the issuer) and id-ppl-independent (inherits nothing and is treated as its own identity). For both, the policy field MUST NOT be present. Any other language marks a restricted proxy.

The RFC does not define a restriction language. It leaves that to the parties who use the extension.
sections.eli5: The permission slip has a name that starts with yours plus a nickname. It also says how many further slips can be made from it and whether it is a full pass, a no-rights pass, or a limited one.

sections.title: Path Validation and Rights
sections.content:
A relying party checks a chain of PCs starting from an EEC that has already passed normal RFC 3280 validation. For each certificate, validation checks the signature, that the validity period includes the current time, that the issuer name matches the previous subject, and that the subject is that name with a CN appended. It processes ProxyCertInfo, tightens the maximum path length where pCPathLenConstraint is smaller, and collects key usage and policies into a policy list that is returned to the application. Implementations need not use the RFC's algorithm, but MUST give equivalent external behavior. The RFC says there is no mechanism defined for revoking proxy certificates.

Rights work as a combination. A PC's rights are the union of rights granted to the PC's own identity and the inherited rights, where inherited rights are the issuer's rights intersected with the proxy policy. The RFC's example: Steve may read and write files A and B, and his PC is limited to files A and C. The PC can use file A, but not B (excluded by policy) and not C (Steve lacks it). If an attribute authority separately grants the PC read access to file D, it can read D too.

If the application cannot parse a policy in the chain, it MUST NOT use the subject name of any earlier certificate in the chain for authorization. Effective key usage can only shrink along a chain, except for independent PCs.
sections.eli5: The guard checks every signature in the chain, one link at a time. Your helper can only do what both you and your note allow, so the note can shrink your powers but never grow them.

sections.title: Commentary: Attribute Certificates and Tracing
sections.content:
Section 5 is non-normative commentary. It compares PCs with Attribute Certificates (ACs), which bind an attribute to an identity via an attribute authority. ACs from a third party work equally well with an EEC or a PC. For delegation, the RFC says an AC-based design would require all protocols and authorization services to understand ACs and would require the delegator to know in advance every identity to be granted rights, whereas PCs can be delegated onward without the originating EEC knowing. It adds that reasonable arguments exist for either approach.

It also gives examples, such as a third-party FTP transfer between two servers, and a restricted case where a process may only read file F1 on host H1 and write file F2 on host H2. The RFC says delegation tracing, meaning recording who delegated to whom, was considered but left out because agreement had not been reached.
sections.eli5: There is another way to give permission, using separate badges. The authors say your own slip is easier to pass along, but both ways are reasonable.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A PC is generally less secure than the EEC that issued it, since its private key is often protected only by file system security so that single sign-on works. Still, a compromised PC cannot sign an EEC or a PC for another user, can be misused only for its lifetime and within its policy, and does not compromise the EEC key. The RFC suggests limiting validity to no longer than needed and including a restriction policy.

An issuer can use pCPathLenConstraint to limit further delegation, and can only remove key usage bits, never add them back. Relying parties place trust in the Proxy Issuers in the chain, since nothing enforces unique subject names. The RFC also warns that receiving delegation requires generating a key pair, which can be exploited for denial of service, so the delegating party should be authenticated. With a central repository holding EEC private keys, the RFC strongly suggests a hardware module and notes that compromise of the repository is serious. Revoking an issued PC can use the CRL Distribution Points extension or OCSP.
sections.eli5: The note is easier to steal than your real keys, so make it expire fast and limit what it allows. If it is stolen, your real keys are still safe.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has established a registry for proxy policy languages. Registration in the IETF space requires IETF standards action. Private languages should live under organizational OIDs, and their authors are encouraged to list them in the registry with a pointer to a specification. The registry starts with two entries: 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.21.1 for id-ppl-inheritALL and 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.21.2 for id-ppl-independent.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of the kinds of permission slips, and the two basic kinds are already on it.
